title: Autonomic scaling + cache eviction: customer notice and post-incident summary
summary_for_statuspage: Partial degradation of inference latency for a subset of tenants between 2029-10-30 03:12–04:45 UTC caused by coordinated cache eviction and rapid autoscaler pod churn. Short-term mitigations restored service; engineering is rolling a permanent fix. No model or user data integrity impacted.
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a customer-facing draft that we will publish to the status page and email to affected tenants. It explains what happened, who was affected, what we did to restore service, and the actions we will take to prevent recurrence. Intended audience: application engineers and platform leads who rely on Redwood inference for production traffic.

Executive summary:
On 2029-10-30 between approximately 03:12 and 04:45 UTC, some customers experienced increased token latency and occasional client-side timeouts for short-running generation requests. The impact affected predominantly small and mid-size tenants that had predictive caching enabled and were routed to the predictive-autoscaling pool in the us-west region. The root cause was an interaction between a background LRU compaction job in the KV cache and a newly deployed predictive autoscaler that led to rapid GPU pod churn and large-scale cache evictions. This produced a wave of cold-cache misses and transient queueing.

What customers saw:
- Increased 95th/99th percentile generation latency for short prompts (0.5–3s typical baseline increased to 2–8s)
- Intermittent request timeouts for some tenants with conservative client-side timeouts
- No loss or corruption of input data, no unauthorized access, no dropped tokens beyond transient retries

Timeline (UTC, all times approximate):
- 03:10 – Predictive autoscaler rollout (canary) begins for us-west pool (non-traffic Canary green check completed)
- 03:12 – First elevated latency alerts for short-tail requests detected by synthetic monitors
- 03:18 – On-call SRE begins investigation; dashboards show increased pod churn and cache hit-rate collapse
- 03:25 – Engineering determines correlation between LRU compaction runs and autoscaler downscales. Cache compaction had been made more aggressive in a recent runtime optimization change (PR #2148).
- 03:30 – Immediate mitigations activated (see below)
- 03:40 – Autoscaler rollback initiated to stable algorithm; background compaction rate reduced to prior settings
- 04:05 – Cache warmup helpers (pre-warm for highest-traffic tenants) enabled; pod churn subsides
- 04:45 – Latency and error rates back to baseline; monitoring verifies stable behavior across tenants

Root cause analysis (concise):
Two changes were operating together in production for the first time: an aggressive LRU compaction parameter intended to reduce memory usage on the KV cache, and a predictive autoscaler that aggressively right-sized GPU pods based on short-term forecasts. When compaction freed a large portion of cached prefix/KV entries, many requests became cold and required recomputation of large KV footprints. The predictive autoscaler interpreted the short-lived spike pattern as reduced demand and initiated scale-downs, which caused further cache loss and additional cold misses — creating a feedback loop (pod churn -> cache eviction -> spike -> scale decisions) that amplified latency and produced transient client failures.

Immediate mitigations we took:
- Rolled back the predictive autoscaler to the previous stable algorithm (completed by 03:40 UTC).
- Temporarily reverted the aggressive compaction parameter to the prior safe value (03:30–03:40 UTC window).
- Enabled a short "cache grace" window that marks recently-evicted prefixes as candidates for soft-retention to prevent cascade evictions.
- Manually triggered cache warmups for the heaviest affected tenants and temporarily provisioned extra headroom in the us-west pool while observations validated stability.
- Raised short-term capacity headroom across predictive pools for the next 12 hours to avoid tight autoscaling thresholds.

Customer impact and scope:
- Affected customers: ~7% of active tenants routed to the predictive-autoscaling pool in us-west; primarily tenants with small steady-state footprints but bursty short requests and prefix caching enabled.
- Duration: transient impact lasting ~1.5 hours, with full stabilization by 04:45 UTC.
- Data integrity: none. No model artifacts or user data were lost or exposed.
- SLA: We are evaluating whether this incident meets the criteria for an SLO credit. If so, affected subscribers will be contacted with a compensation proposal.

Permanent fixes and timeline:
- Short term (1–3 days): publish conservative defaults for compaction and autoscaler interaction; add a circuit-breaker to prevent simultaneous aggressive compaction + aggressive scale decisions. (Owner: runtime team, PR queued)
- Medium term (2–4 weeks): instrument autoscaler with cache-awareness signals (cache-hit rate hysteresis) so scale decisions consider expected KV warmup cost. Add a predictive warm-start flow for small tenants. (Owner: serving-runtime / autoscale squad)
- Long term (1–3 months): refine predictive models and introduce a cross-layer coordination layer in the control plane such that cache compaction, prefetch, and scaling policies are evaluated together before applying disruptive changes. (Owner: platform engineering)

What you can do as a customer (recommended immediate actions):
- If you run with client-side timeouts under 5s, consider increasing to 8–10s temporarily if you saw timeouts; our backend retries safely for idempotent generation requests.
- If you have strict latency constraints, pin traffic to dedicated pools (Redwood Dedicated) or request a temporary increase in headroom from your TAM/CSM while fixes are validated.
- If you would like us to pre-warm prefixes for high-value routes during the mitigation window, open a ticket with your account team (we can prioritize warmups).

Communication plan and next messages:
- Status page summary (short) will go live now with the short impact blurb and a link to this post-incident summary draft.
- A follow-up technical postmortem will be published within 7 working days with metrics, RCA artifacts, and verification runbooks.
- Customer Success will proactively reach out to the small set of heavily impacted tenants to offer direct support and to coordinate any headroom or warmup needs.

Contact and support:
- Primary contact: Aisha Patel (Customer Success lead) — aisha.patel@redwood.ai
- Engineering liaison: Liam Chen (SRE) — liam.chen@redwood.ai
- For urgent tenant-level assistance open a ticket via the support portal and reference: JIRA-OP-4927.

Apology and closing note:
We apologize for the interruption and the impact on your application performance. Our priority is to ensure predictable, high-quality inference for production workloads; we take incidents like this seriously and will follow through on the remediation and preventive actions described above.

Appendix: technical artifacts (internal links)
- Incident runbook timeline and raw metrics: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/INC-2029-10-autoscale-cache-compaction
- Rollback PR and runtime revert: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2148
- Autoscaler tuning proposal: JIRA-OP-4927

Draft notes for reviewers:
- Confirm the short statuspage blurb is concise and non-technical; leave the body here for customers who want engineering detail.
- Check SLA/compensation flow with legal and finance before including a formal credits offer.
- If approved, we will publish an edited postmortem (remove internal links to debug traces) and notify affected tenants via the support portal and their CSMs.
